statement: In two small studies of people who had used ecstasy, both from the 1990s and without a comparison group, people described MDMA as often raising sexual desire or feelings of closeness and sensuality while making erections and orgasm harder for some: in a retrospective survey of 35 people who had used MDMA before sex, all reported more desire and 32 more satisfaction, 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women a delayed orgasm, and 8 of 20 men weaker erections while another 8 reported stronger ones; in interviews with 98 people, a slight majority described closeness rather than sexual desire. These are recollections of self-selected people, not measurements, so they cannot show how often any of this happens among people who take MDMA, or that MDMA rather than other drugs, expectations or the people themselves caused it. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (two independent studies agree on the kinds of experiences, not on how often). In Israel, 20 men aged 22 to 46 and 15 women aged 21 to 48 who had occasionally used MDMA before a sexual encounter, healthy, medication-free and without sexual or major psychiatric disorders, rated sex in the 6 hours after MDMA against their usual sex without it, from -3 (profound decrease) to +3 (profound increase), in a structured interview (9 by telephone); how and when they were recruited is not stated, and what their pills contained was not known (Zemishlany et al., 2001). All 35 reported more desire, 34 of them a moderate or profound increase, and most described sex as more sensual than usual; 32 rated satisfaction moderately or profoundly higher (18 of 20 men, 14 of 15 women). Of the 20 men, 8 rated erections worse (4 of them moderately or profoundly), 8 better and 4 unchanged; 12 of 15 women reported more lubrication and 2 less. Orgasm was delayed for 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women, and 1 man and 2 women could not reach orgasm at all on MDMA, while orgasm felt more intense to 17 men and 8 women. All 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm still rated satisfaction moderately or profoundly higher (editors' tally from the paper's table of every person's ratings). With 20 men, the 95% interval around 8 of 20 runs from about 22 to 61 in 100 (editors' calculation). Ten men and 10 women had sometimes taken cannabis with MDMA; the authors say the ratings referred to MDMA alone and did not differ by cannabis use, but print no data. The paper's summary reports the 40 in 100 men with worse erections but not the 40 in 100 with better ones, and its conclusion that MDMA impairs sexual performance rests mostly on delayed orgasm in people who still rated sex as more satisfying; the authors themselves say that expectations may shape such reports. In Northern Ireland, 98 people who used or had used ecstasy were interviewed in depth in 1997 and 1998 (69 in 100 men; aged 17 to 45; 44 in 100 had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions), recruited through notices, a club magazine, local agencies, the interviewers' contacts, referral by other respondents and paid recruiters, but not in clubs; the findings are themes illustrated by quotations, with no counts and no description of how the interviews were analysed (McElrath, 2005). A slight majority described ecstasy as more about sensuality and deep emotions than sexual desire; some men who tried to have sex described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, which seemed to affect men aged 25 or younger more often; other men and women described strongly heightened desire and very good sex; the author suggests that differences in sexual interest between people may explain the range. Some of those who had sex during ecstasy episodes, more often those aged 18 to 25, described multiple partners, one-night stands with strangers or acquaintances, and regret the next day; condoms were rarely used during ecstasy episodes with intercourse, but few respondents used them when no drugs had been taken either, so the study cannot show that MDMA made sex riskier; respondents' views were mixed on whether ecstasy or alcohol led to more risk, and alcohol and other drugs were often taken in the same episodes. The author says the scene has probably changed since 1997 and 1998. Neither study tested the pills, measured sexual function directly or compared occasions with and without MDMA as they happened; the Israeli sample was chosen for having used MDMA before sex, which may be why everyone there reported more desire while a slight majority of the Northern Irish sample described closeness rather than desire (editors' reading).
plain: What does MDMA do to sex? Two small studies from the 1990s asked people about it, with no comparison group and no testing of their pills. In Israel, 35 people who had taken MDMA before sex compared it, from memory, with their usual sex: all said desire went up, 32 said they were more satisfied, and most said sex felt more sensual. But orgasm took longer for 16 of the 20 men and 6 of the 15 women, and 3 people could not reach orgasm at all. Of the 20 men, 8 said erections were weaker, 8 said stronger and 4 noticed no change. In interviews with 98 people in Northern Ireland, a slight majority said MDMA was more about closeness than sex; some men said they could not get an erection, while others described strong desire and very good sex. Some described one-night stands and regret the next day; condoms were rarely used on ecstasy, but few used them without drugs either. These are people's memories, so they cannot show how often any of this happens or that MDMA alone caused it.
population: People who had used ecstasy, in two self-selected samples: 35 in Israel (20 men aged 22 to 46, 15 women aged 21 to 48) who had occasionally used MDMA before sex, healthy, medication-free and without sexual or major psychiatric disorders, recruitment not described; 98 current or former users in Northern Ireland interviewed in 1997 and 1998 (69% men; aged 17 to 45; 16% gay or bisexual), recruited through notices, a magazine, agencies, contacts, referral and paid recruiters
exposure: MDMA as ecstasy tablets or pills taken by people's own choice, content and amount unknown and not tested (self-reported; in Israel, cannabis sometimes taken with MDMA by 20 of the 35; in Northern Ireland, alcohol and other drugs often taken in the same episodes)
comparator: Each person's memory of their usual sex without MDMA (Israel); none in Northern Ireland, where respondents compared experiences in their own words
outcome: Recalled sexual desire, erection or lubrication, delay and intensity of orgasm, and satisfaction, each rated from -3 to +3 against usual function (Israel); themes in interviews on sensuality, desire, sexual performance and sexual risk (Northern Ireland)
magnitude: Zemishlany et al. (2001), Table I (20 men, 15 women; counts by the editors from the per-person ratings, which match the text's percentages): desire up 35 of 35, moderately or profoundly 34; satisfaction moderately or profoundly up 32 of 35 (Wilson 95% interval 78% to 97%, editors' calculation), men 18 of 20, women 14 of 15; erection worse 8 of 20 men (22% to 61%; 4 moderately or profoundly), better 8, unchanged 4; lubrication more 12 of 15 women (55% to 93%), less 2, unchanged 1; orgasm delayed 16 of 20 men (58% to 92%) and 6 of 15 women (20% to 64%); no orgasm on MDMA 1 man and 2 women; orgasm more intense 17 of 20 men and 8 of 15 women, less intense 1 man and 3 women; satisfaction +2 or +3 in all 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people without orgasm; cannabis sometimes with MDMA 10 men and 10 women; interviewed by telephone 9 (printed 25%; 9 of 35 is 26%, editors' calculation). McElrath (2005): 98 interviewed (106, 8 discarded); themes only, no counts ('a slight majority' described sensuality or deep emotions rather than sexual desire).

evidence.locator: Summary (p. 127); Subjects and methods, 1st paragraph (p. 127, continuing on p. 128) and 2nd paragraph (p. 128); Table I, age column (p. 129)
evidence.extracted: Short communication from Geha Psychiatric Hospital and Tel Aviv University, Israel. 20 men and 15 women who had occasionally used MDMA before a sexual encounter agreed to a structured interview (9 by telephone) about sex up to 6 hours after taking it; how they were recruited, and when, is not described. Included only people who were physically healthy, without a major psychiatric disorder or history of sexual disorders, not abusing alcohol or opiates and medication-free; all had earlier recreational MDMA experience; 94% had high school or academic education. Desire, erection (lubrication in women), orgasm intensity and delay, and satisfaction were each rated against the person's usual function from -3 (profound decrease) to +3 (profound increase); the ratings are retrospective self-reports. Ages 21 to 48 (men 22 to 46, women 21 to 48).

evidence.extracted: All 35 reported increased desire, moderate to profound in 19 of 20 men and all 15 women; most described sex as more sensual than usual; satisfaction moderately to profoundly increased in 90% of men and 93% of women (18 of 20 and 14 of 15 in Table I). Erection: 40% of men reported a negative and 40% a positive effect (8 and 8 of 20; 4 unchanged); lubrication enhanced in 80% of women (12 of 15; 2 decreased). Orgasm delayed in 16 men (80%) and 6 women (40%); 1 man and 2 women could not reach orgasm at all; orgasm more intense for 85% of men and 53% of women (17 and 8). Editors' tally from Table I: of the 8 men with weaker erections, 4 rated the decrease moderate or profound; orgasm less intense for 1 man and 3 women; all 8 men with weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm rated satisfaction +2 or +3; every percentage in the text matches the table. Editors' Wilson 95% intervals: weaker erections 8 of 20, 22% to 61%; delayed orgasm 16 of 20 men, 58% to 92%, and 6 of 15 women, 20% to 64%; satisfaction 32 of 35, 78% to 97%.

evidence.extracted: 10 men and 10 women had sometimes taken cannabis with MDMA, mainly, they said, to raise desire; the ratings were said to refer to MDMA alone, and the authors report no difference in any rating between those who did and did not add cannabis, without data. The Discussion calls the effects on erection inconsistent, while the Summary reports erection impaired in 40% of the men without the 40% who reported better erections, and the conclusion says MDMA seems to impair sexual performance in spite of more desire and greater satisfaction. Limits named by the authors: a sample not randomly selected, of people willing to describe use of an illegal drug; retrospective recall open to inaccuracy; unknown dose and purity of the pills; cannabis use by about half; and expected effects of the drug (a placebo effect), which should not be disregarded.

evidence.extracted: Qualitative study by one author: face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews of 1 to 2 hours, taped and transcribed, with current and former ecstasy users in Northern Ireland, October 1997 to November 1998; 106 interviewed and 8 discarded for recording or transcription problems, leaving 98. Recruited through notices in shops and health centres, a club and music magazine, local agencies (including sexually transmitted disease clinics and gay and lesbian outreach), the interviewers' own contacts, referral by respondents and paid recruiters (10 pounds per referral and completed interview); clubs were not used. 69% men; aged 17 to 45 (mean 25); 16% gay or bisexual; 92% had used ecstasy in the past 6 months and 44% on at least 100 occasions. Effects attributed to MDMA refer to what respondents believed they had taken, as tablet content varies. The article describes no method of analysis and counts no finding.

evidence.extracted: Interactions of MDMA with alcohol and cannabis could not be examined, and the author says prospective data on the timing of drug use and sex would be needed, as recall of heavy multi-drug episodes may be affected. The abstract states findings more strongly than the text: most respondents (the text: a slight majority) reported closeness without wanting penetrative sex; gay and bisexual women in particular had used MDMA for sexual enhancement, which the Discussion says their small number in the sample does not allow to be concluded; and sexual risk taking was prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, without counts and without the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. The data are from 1997 and 1998; the author says the scene has probably changed and that it is unclear whether the findings apply now.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement and selection within each sample: in Israel an unvalidated retrospective rating scale, an unverified exposure of unknown dose and content, interviews partly by telephone by unnamed interviewers, and no stated recruitment, place or dates (card sc_zemishlany_2001, JBI prevalence checklist: high); in Northern Ireland no description of how the interviews were analysed and no counts behind 'a slight majority', 'some' or 'several' (card sc_mcelrath_2005, editors' qualitative checklist: high). The Israeli table lets every count be checked, so one level.

inconsistency.note: The two studies agree on the kinds of experiences (more desire or closeness; erection and orgasm difficulties for some men; heightened desire for others). They differ on desire: all 35 reported more of it in Israel, while in Northern Ireland a slight majority described closeness rather than desire, which the statement explains, as the editors' reading, by the Israeli sample's selection for use before sex.

indirectness.note: Coverage: neither sample has a sampling frame; the Israeli sample was selected for having used MDMA before sex and the Northern Irish one was reached through agencies, contacts and paid referral; both are from the 1990s, and the author of the second says the scene has probably changed.

imprecision.note: Small samples (20 men, 15 women; 95% intervals about 40 points wide around the sex-specific shares, editors' calculation), stated with the counts; the claim is already at the floor.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the people sampled (METHODS 6.3): starts low; risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 give very low, the floor; never upgraded. Status replicated: the Israeli survey and the Northern Irish interviews are independent samples by different teams that agree on the kinds of experiences people describe, not on how often each occurs, which neither can show. Neither study measured sexual function, tested the pills or compared occasions with and without MDMA, so the statement makes no causal claim: what people recalled may reflect the drug, other drugs taken (cannabis for 20 of the 35; alcohol often in Northern Ireland), expectations or the people themselves. The Israeli summary's 'erection impaired in 40%' is given with the other 40% who reported better erections, and the risk accounts are given with the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. Findings only: nothing here is about choosing or using MDMA for sex.

Not read: Buffum and Moser (1986, Journal of Psychoactive Drugs 18, 355-359), the only earlier survey the Israeli authors cite (erectile ability decreased in 46 in 100 men, as cited). No controlled study of MDMA and sexual function, and nothing on MDMA with erection medicines (a safety question people ask), was among the papers on file. Pages: mdma.
